opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to see it is that the digital world is the most natural first environment for agents, because almost everything in it is already expressed in a form a model can read and act on: text, code, web pages, APIs, files. In the physical world you need a body, sensors, actuators, and you're limited by how fast you can collect data. In the digital world, the "body" is basically a set of tools, a browser, a terminal, a code interpreter, a search engine, and the model can use them at the speed of compute.

So my picture is that an agent's interaction with the digital world will move through a few stages. The first stage is what we've already seen: the model answers a question in a single turn, maybe it calls a search tool once. The second stage is long-horizon interaction, where the agent takes dozens or hundreds of steps. It searches, reads, notices that something doesn't add up, goes back, writes some code, runs it, looks at the error, fixes it, and eventually delivers a result that's actually useful, like a full research report or a working piece of software. That's where we are now, and I think the key capability there isn't any single tool, it's the ability to stay coherent over a long trajectory and to self-correct.

The third stage, which I find most exciting, is when the agent isn't just using the digital world but starts to reshape it. It writes its own tools, builds its own environments, maybe even generates the data and tasks it learns from. At that point the boundary between "the model" and "the environment" becomes blurry. The agent is effectively expanding the space of what it can do by itself.

And the reason I care so much about this is related to how I think about scaling. Pre-training on static internet data is running into limits; the high-quality tokens are finite. But interaction is a way to generate new, high-value data that didn't exist before. Every time an agent attempts a hard task in a real environment and gets feedback, success or failure, that's a signal you can learn from. So the digital world isn't just where agents are deployed, it's also where they get trained. Reinforcement learning on top of these long interactions is, I think, one of the most important paths for continuing to push intelligence forward.

Of course there are real challenges. Many digital environments weren't designed for agents; they're designed for humans clicking around with a mouse, with CAPTCHAs, unstable interfaces, and things like that. Reward is often hard to define for open-ended tasks. And when an agent can take real actions, like sending an email or modifying a file, safety and controllability matter a lot more than when it's just producing text. But I'm fairly optimistic. I think over the next few years, a lot of knowledge work will be something you delegate to an agent with a goal rather than step-by-step instructions, and the digital world will gradually become more agent-native as a result.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents writing and running code and creating their own tools as part of interacting with the digital world.

r002.rationale: It lists examples of digital tools but does not characterize their distribution as long-tailed.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most important thing to understand is that the digital world is, for an AI, the most natural environment it could possibly live in. A human has to use eyes and hands to deal with a screen, but for a model, everything on a computer is already information. The browser, the terminal, the file system, APIs, software interfaces — all of it is text, pixels, structured data. So in a sense, the digital world is the native habitat of an agent, in a way the physical world is not, at least not yet.

The way I think about it, there are roughly three layers. The first is perception: can the agent actually see what's on the screen, read a page, understand the state of a piece of software? Two or three years ago this was hard. Today, with multimodal models, it's mostly solved — the model can look at a screenshot and tell you what it is, or read a long document and extract what matters.

The second layer is action. Can it click, type, run a command, call an API, and keep doing that reliably over many steps? This is where things get interesting, because the difficulty isn't any single action. It's the compounding of errors. If each step is 99% right, after a hundred steps you're at something like 37%. So what we really care about is long-horizon reliability — the ability to work for an hour, or a day, without drifting off course. That's a training problem much more than it is a prompting problem. You need reinforcement learning on real tasks, with real feedback from the environment, so the model learns to notice when it's wrong and recover.

The third layer, which I think people underestimate, is autonomy and judgment. Interacting with the digital world isn't just executing instructions. It's deciding what to look at, what to verify, when to stop and ask, when the goal has actually been achieved versus when it merely looks achieved. A good human engineer doesn't just run the code — they run the tests, read the output, and doubt themselves at the right moments. That kind of self-correction loop is what separates a tool from an agent.

Where I think this goes: the keyboard and mouse will eventually be a transitional interface. Right now we make agents imitate humans, clicking through GUIs designed for people. That's useful because it gives immediate access to all existing software. But over time, more and more software will expose itself in ways designed for agents, and agents will talk to agents. The entire internet starts to look less like pages for humans to read and more like a space for models to operate in.

So the vision, if I had to compress it, is this: an agent should be able to do anything on a computer that a capable person could do, over arbitrarily long time spans, and gradually do things no single person could — because it can read everything, try many things in parallel, and never gets tired. The gap between today and that vision is mostly about long-horizon reliability and taste. And I think both of those are learnable.

astra-6.text:
I think an agent should be able to do more than answer questions. You should be able to give it a goal, and it should figure out what information it needs, which tools to use, and how to carry out the task. That could mean interacting with a browser, writing and running code, or working across different applications.

The important part is the feedback loop. It takes an action, observes what happened, and adjusts its next step. If something fails, it needs to understand why and try another approach. That’s what allows it to move beyond generating a plausible plan to actually completing work.

I also think it needs to know when to involve you. For routine steps, it can act independently. When your intent is ambiguous or a decision has significant consequences, it should ask. The goal is for you to communicate what you want to accomplish without having to specify every click along the way.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize the available tools as long-tailed.

r003.rationale: It does not say that strong generalization enables using previously unseen tools.

sol-6.1.text:
I think an agent should be able to move from understanding what you want to actually carrying it out in the digital world. Today, that interaction is often limited to generating text. But an agent could use software, navigate interfaces, retrieve information, and coordinate multiple steps toward a goal.

The important part is closing the loop. It takes an action, observes what happened, and adjusts its next step. If something fails, it needs to recognize that and recover. And when your intent is ambiguous, or an action has significant consequences, it should ask you.

So I envision interaction becoming more goal-oriented. You describe the outcome you want, and the agent handles more of the execution, while giving you visibility and control.
